name: Jade Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Oakmere Farm for my uncle Kenji, 250 hectares with 12,000 free-range laying hens, 300 ewes, and wheat and oilseed rape. I own a fifth of it, which my grandmother left me, and Uncle Kenji has no children, so the plan is that I take it over. My day starts at half five in the egg packing room, then the flock checks, then the farm shop and our egg vending machines in three villages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love building things, and in the last two years I've doubled the egg sales through the shop and the machines. I use AI every day, for egg sales forecasts, the shop's social media, and cameras in the hen houses that flag a sick bird. What drains me is government rules that take six months to approve a new shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a shame, but we'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were still worth having, and I'd keep using them. At church and the young farmers' club I'd say the work's still the work. Online I'd post about what saved us time, because some people would give up too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means Oakmere grows the way I'd planned anyway. I own a fifth of the farm, I'm well paid, and I've got savings on top. My real frustrations are the planning rules and the big supermarkets squeezing egg prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the camera system and the forecasting. I'd put a fourth egg vending machine in the next village this spring. And I'd apply for permission to build a second laying shed, which would take forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the supermarkets. How much do they squeeze you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We sell a third of our eggs to a supermarket packer, and they cut the price twice last year. That's why I built the shop and the machines, so we're not at their mercy. Every egg sold at the gate is worth twice an egg sold to a supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Uncle Kenji feel about all the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I'm mad, but he can't argue with the numbers. He still walks the hen houses every evening, and I'm glad he does. The cameras don't replace a man who's kept hens for forty years.

say: I'd say the tools are still **worth having**.
I'd post about what **saved time** so others don't give up early.
think: Privately Oakmere grows **as planned**, with my **fifth share** secure.
My frustrations are **planning rules** and supermarket egg prices.
do: Keep the **hen cameras** and sales forecasting running.
Install a fourth **egg vending machine** this spring.
Apply to build a **second laying shed**.
S0.quote: Every egg sold at the gate is worth twice an egg sold to a supermarket.
fieldNote: She's an **owner-manager** whose income is secure.
She blames **planning rules** and big retailers, not technology.
Direct sales are her answer to **price squeeze**.
She respects her uncle's **experience** alongside her tools.

steps.text: Keep the hen-house cameras and egg sales forecasts running
Install a fourth egg vending machine in the next village

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've been hoping for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for family farms to compete with the big ones. At the young farmers' club I'd show people what I use. I'd also say the government should get out of the way and let farmers try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get more done with fewer evenings at the laptop. The shop orders, the bookkeeping and the social media would run themselves. I'd worry a bit about Sarah, who does our shop and accounts part-time, but I'd move her onto customer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in AI for all the ordering and the accounts within six months. I'd buy an egg-collecting robot for one shed, because they're already sold and I've seen them work. And I'd put Sarah on a course to run the shop's customer side, paid by the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sarah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the farm needs her, just doing different things. She's 50 and she knows every customer by name. Software can do the books, but Sarah is the reason people come back to the farm shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from automating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shepherding. Uncle Kenji and I do the ewes ourselves, and I wouldn't want a robot with them yet. Some things are part of who we are, not just jobs.

say: I'd call it a **chance** for family farms to compete.
I'd say government should **get out** of farmers' way.
think: Privately I'd win back **evenings** from the laptop.
I'd worry about **Sarah's** office work but move her to customers.
do: Move **ordering and accounts** onto AI within six months.
Buy an **egg-collecting robot** for one shed.

fieldNote: She automates fast but **protects** her part-time worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance, but we need to make sure families and villages don't fall apart. At church I'd say we look after each other. I'd want the council to fund apprenticeships, not just benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the farm's fine, I own part of it and the robots would cut our costs. But the village would change, with the young lads on the farms out of work by 2031. I'd worry about the church, the school, the shop, all the things that need people living here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy robots for the hen houses as soon as they're good, maybe 2031. I'd start an apprenticeship for two village teenagers now, teaching them farm robots and hens, so they've got a skill when it comes. And I'd lobby the council to fast-track robot sheds and fund more apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm's fine. Would you be employing fewer people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. We have seven staff now, and by 2032 we might need three. I'd try to find the others work on the farm or help them train. But I won't pretend I'd keep paying people to do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that in tension with wanting the village to survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I don't have a neat answer. A village needs people with jobs, and I can't make jobs out of nothing. The best I can do is train the young ones, so they're the ones fixing the robots.

say: I'd call it a **big chance** if families and villages hold together.
I'd want the council to fund **apprenticeships**, not just benefits.
think: Privately Oakmere is fine; robots would **cut our costs**.
I'd worry about the **village**: church, school and shop need people.
do: Buy **hen-house robots** as soon as they're good, around 2031.
Start an **apprenticeship** now for two village teenagers.
Lobby the council to **fast-track** robot sheds and apprenticeships.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, for others rather than herself.
S2.quote: A village needs people with jobs, and I can't make jobs out of nothing.
fieldNote: Her own income is **secure**; her worry is the **community**.
She openly expects to cut staff from **seven to three**.
She names the **tension** between business and village life.
Her answer is **training** the young, not subsidies.

steps.text: Buy robots for the hen houses around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a good amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it properly, so let's plan. At the young farmers' club I'd talk about robots and apprenticeships. I'd be positive in public, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can build Oakmere into something bigger before the robots come in 2034. I'd be in charge by then, with Uncle Kenji retired. It's a good timeline for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the second laying shed, designed for robots from the start. I'd rent out our egg-collecting robot to two neighbouring farms. And I'd start the apprenticeship for village teenagers, with more time to do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the 300 ewes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep them by hand, with Uncle Kenji, as long as he wants. When he's gone, I don't know. That's the one part I can't think about too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever sell Oakmere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My grandmother would come back to haunt me. I'd rather run Oakmere with robots than sell it to someone who'd never set foot on it.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan** properly, so let's plan.
I'd talk positively about **robots and apprenticeships** at the young farmers' club.
think: Privately five years lets me **grow Oakmere** bigger before the 2034 robots.
I'd be **in charge** by then, with Uncle Kenji retired.

Run the village **apprenticeship** with more time to do it well.
S3.quote: I'd rather run Oakmere with robots than sell it to someone who'd never set foot on it.
fieldNote: The five-year window suits her **growth plans**.
She keeps the **ewes** by hand as a family tie.

steps.text: Build a robot-ready second laying shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready has only themselves to blame. Maybe that sounds harsh, but I'd say it. I'd also say families and churches should help people get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is easy for me. I'd be running Oakmere with robots by 2039, probably married with kids. The village would have time to adjust too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the farm as now. I'd keep up with new tools and buy robots when they're ready. And I'd plan a family without changing the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who aren't ready have themselves to blame. Would you say that to Sarah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not to Sarah. I'd help Sarah, she's family to us. I suppose it's easier to say about strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to grow up on Oakmere, knowing hens and sheep and how the robots work. Faith, family and a trade.

I'd say **families and churches** should help people prepare.
think: Privately I'd be running Oakmere with **robots** by 2039.
I'd likely be **married with kids**, with the village adjusted.
do: Plan a **family** without changing the timing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for me but for the village, because the young people would lose farm work before they'd learned anything else. What would help is apprenticeships paid for by the council, and faster planning approval so farms can grow and take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the old people. Uncle Kenji and the older farmers have knowledge the robots will never have. A robot can collect eggs, but it took Uncle Kenji forty years to know when a hen is about to go off lay.

headlineQuote: A robot can collect eggs, but it took Uncle Kenji forty years to know when a hen is about to go off lay.
portrait: Jade is 27, **manages** and part-owns her uncle's egg, sheep and arable farm, which she will inherit.
She uses **AI** every day and has doubled sales through a farm shop and **vending machines**.
She blames **planning rules** and supermarkets, and wants apprenticeships rather than benefits.
Her own income stays **secure** in every scenario; her worry is the **village**.
She automates eagerly but keeps the **ewes** by hand with her uncle.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because village **youth** lose farm work too soon.
whatWouldHelp: **Council-paid apprenticeships** and faster **planning approval** for farm growth.
